To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the radius of curvature of the semicircular canals is proportional to the body mass of the animal (i.e., the smaller the animal, the smaller the semicircular canal) and that the proportionality constant for the fish is different from that of the mammals.
the size of semicircular canals scales with body mass in fossil fish and Recent teleosts in the same manner, but differs in fossil amphibians and Recent mammals.

(i) semicircular canal size is correlated with body mass, (ii) this correlation is different for teleosts, mammals, and fossil amphibians, and (iii) semicircular canals are smaller in tetrapods than fish.

the evolution of the vestibular system, and the relationship between the size of the semicircular canals and body mass in fossil fishes and labyrinthodont amphibians, and in modern fishes, amphibians and mammals.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
semicircular canal size in fishes and amphibians was not significantly different in the past than it is today.
semicircular canals in fossil fishes were more sensitive than those of Recent fish, but were less sensitive than those of modern tetrapods.
the semicircular canal system of fossil fishes is similar to that of Recent fishes, but the system in fossil labyrinthodont amphibian is similar to that in Recent mammals.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, although the semicircular canals of fossil vertebrates are not well understood in detail, the general pattern of semicircular canal size and body mass is similar to that of Recent vertebrates.
semicircular canal morphology is not a reliable indicator of the sensory capabilities of the inner ear in extinct vertebrates.

the fossil record is now rich enough to allow the construction of semicircular canal size-body mass regressions in several extinct vertebrate groups.
